newsitem.title: USA: Ralston expected to withdraw name for top US post.
newsitem.headline: Ralston expected to withdraw name for top US post.

text.p: Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston is expected to withdraw from consideration to become chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in a controversy over an adulterous affair he had years ago, Pentagon officials said on Sunday.

Ralston, 56, was scheduled to discuss the matter with Defence Secretary William Cohen on Monday amid warnings from Congress that the Senate might reject Ralston if he were to be nominted to become the nation's new top military officer by President Bill Clinton.

"I believe that there's been such a cloud created in this climate as we're looking into the issues of sexual misconduct that it would be very difficult for him to be confirmed before the U.S. Senate," said Representative Steve Buyer, the Indiana Republican who heads the House subcommittee on Military Personnel.
Buyer, on the NBC programme "Meet the Press," said he anticipated Ralston would take his name out of consideration.

"This has become much, much bigger than one general now," a Pentagon official who asked not to be identified told Reuters. "I expect he will withdraw for the good of the military even though he had earlier planned to fight this thing out."
But Caspar Weinberger, who was defence secretary under President Ronald Reagan, said Cohen should stand by Ralston if Ralston was indeed his first choice for the job.
"I would stand by him as I think Secretary Cohen has tried to do," Weinberger said on the ABC programme "This Week."

Setting off a heated controversy, Cohen and the White House said last week that Ralston remained high in the running despite his admission that he had an adulterous affair while separated from his first wife 13 years ago. They subsequently divorced.

Ralston, who is vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs, until recently had been the favourite to replace Army Gen. John Shalikashvili as chairman when Shalikashvili retires on Sept. 30. The Senate must approve the person who takes his place.

Angry members of Congress said Cohen's explanation of his continued support for Ralston was not good enough only weeks after the Air Force forced its first woman bomber pilot, Lt. Kelly Flinn, to resign to avoid a court-martial on charges of adultery and other serious accusations.
Republican Sen. Olympia Snow of Maine, the only woman on the Armed Services Committee, said on ABC that Ralston would face "tough questions, obviously."
Asked whether the possible future nomination would be rejected by the Senate, she replied: "Not necessarily. I mean I think it's going to face a rocky road."
"I think you can read the writing on the wall when you look at this," said one senior defence official on Sunday. "It would be a tough fight (in Congress) at the least."
Ralston returned on Sunday from a military visit to former Soviet republics in central Asia. He made no comment on his return and, so far, he has given no indication that he intends to withdraw.
Cohen is scheduled to begin an eight-day visit to Europe and the Gulf next Thursday. One senior official said he was not expected to recommend a nominee to Clinton until after he returns.

Published reports said Cohen was looking closely at Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Charles Krulak and Army Gen. Wesley Clark. Also reported earlier to be high on the list was Marine Corps Gen. John Sheehan, based in Norfolk, Virginia, as head of the U.S. Atlantic Command.

The Ralston case has brought to a head months of bitter controversy over reports of martial cheating by high-level military officers as well as an Army scandal over rape and sexual harassment of young female recruits by male drill sergeants at training bases.
